connector: Harriet has brought her brothers and her parents out of Maryland. But in 1850 Congress passes a new law, and runaways living in the North can be caught and sent back. As you read Chapter 13, test each link: did the law cause what happens next, or did it only come first?

a.raw: harriet traveled secretly each night her route stretched far across many states
a.fixed: Harriet traveled secretly each night. Her route stretched far across many states.
a.why: Capital H on Harriet; a period ends the first sentence; capital H starts the second. Secretly tells how she traveled; far tells where the route stretched.

b.raw: the train rolled slowly over the bridge the people shouted joyfully in canada
b.fixed: The train rolled slowly over the bridge. The people shouted joyfully in Canada.
b.why: Capital T starts each sentence; a period ends the first; capital C on Canada (a country). Slowly and joyfully are adverbs that tell how.

fill1.h1: Pushing a button down. Which root means push?
fill1.why: press means push: de + press = push down.

fill2.h1: Holding in a sneeze pushes it under. Which root means push?
fill2.why: press means push: sup + press = push under, hide.

fill3.h1: Keeping a garden in good shape means holding it steady. Which root means hold?
fill3.why: tain means hold: main + tain = hold steady.

fill4.h1: To get something, you take hold of it. Which root means hold?
fill4.why: tain means hold: ob + tain = take hold of.

g4w22cf1.h1: How did the family talk so the neighbors would not hear? Look at the word bank.

g4w22cf2.h1: Which word in the bank tells when, all at once, with no warning?
g4w22cf2.why: Suddenly tells when the dogs began to bark.

g4w22cf3.h1: How would you fold and hide a paper so nobody noticed?
g4w22cf3.why: carefully tells how she folded and hid it.

g4w22cf4.h1: How many times did they use the same route? Look for a word that means not once.
g4w22cf4.why: never tells how often: not even once.

s4w22cf1.h1: create ends in a silent e. What happens to the e before -ive?
s4w22cf1.why: Drop the silent e: create + ive = creative.

s4w22cf2.h1: practice ends in a silent e too. Keep the c, drop the e, add -al.

s4w22cf3.h1: history ends in y. The y drops before -ic.

s4w22cf4.h1: nation already ends in a consonant. Does anything drop?

notes.wgrd: Not everything that comes next was caused by what came before. Line up two events and try ‘because’ between them. If it doesn’t hold up, it only came next.
vocab: The act of ending something, especially slavery.
A guide on the Underground Railroad; or, the person who runs a train.
To make a thought, feeling, or idea known to others.
notes.wordParts: press means “push” and tain means “hold”: express, impress, contain, obtain.
notes.grammar: Two adverbs propping up a weak verb can often become one strong verb. A strong verb shows how without the extra words.
notes.spelling: The suffixes -ive, -al, and -ic turn a word into a describing word: act → active, music → musical, hero → heroic. Look at the base word first. Sometimes a letter drops, like a silent e.

catcher.title: Cause, or only next?
catcher.intro: Pick two events from Ch. 13, an earlier one and a later one. Test them.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: pushing, or holding?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, finishes a patchwork quilt, the family’s only treasure. Years later, in Chapter 12, Harriet tucks that same quilt over her parents’ legs as she drives them out of slavery. press means push, and tain means hold. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: Old Rit’s quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. press = push, tain = hold.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. In 1850, Congress passed a new law, and suddenly the North wasn’t safe for anyone who had run away. Chapter 13 is called The Lion’s Paw. Hold that title in your head. Today’s question: if freedom keeps moving farther away, how far will Harriet go?
transcripts.read: This chapter starts big, with a law, then zooms in on Harriet’s people. Follow the route north in your head, all the way across New York. Watch for friends along the way, and a train ride over roaring water. And look for Josiah Bailey. He’s my favorite person in this book.
transcripts.grammar: Here’s a writer’s trick. When a sentence needs two little helper words to show how someone moved, the verb underneath is usually too weak. Swap in one strong verb, and the helpers can go. Say both versions out loud. Which one sounds like someone sneaking past a guard?

virtue.title: Freedom log
virtue.intro: In Chapter 13, freedom means getting all the way to Canada. Tap the moment you think shows freedom best.

options.t: The train crosses the bridge at Niagara Falls, and the runaways shout, “We’re free! We’ve shook the lion’s paw!”
In the first hard winter in St. Catharines, Harriet chops wood, cooks, and nurses her people.
Harriet’s brothers own land, vote, and send their children to school in St. Catharines.
Josiah Bailey stands up on the train and sings, “One more soul got safe.”
